nameStory: This cheerful spring flower gets its "glory-of-the-snow" name because it blooms so early in the year that it often pushes right up through the last patches of snow. The "Boissier's" part honors Swiss botanist Pierre Edmond Boissier, though it's actually named after his wife Lucile - making it one of the few flowers with a woman's name hidden in its scientific title!
description: Boissier's Glory-of-the-snow is a small spring bulb that produces delicate star-shaped flowers in shades of blue, white, or pink. This petite perennial grows only 4-6 inches tall, sending up slender stems topped with clusters of upward-facing blooms. Each flower has six pointed petals that spread wide open like tiny stars. After blooming in early spring, the entire plant disappears underground until next year, spending most of its life as a dormant bulb.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Six-petaled star-shaped flowers that face upward, typically pale blue with white centers, though can be pure white or pinkish. Each flower is about half an inch across and has a sweet, honey-like fragrance that's strongest on warm days.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Two to three narrow, strap-like leaves that emerge from the ground at the same time as the flowers. The leaves feel smooth and slightly waxy, with a deep green color and prominent parallel veins running lengthwise.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms small colonies over time as bulbs multiply underground. Plants are very short, rarely exceeding 6 inches tall, and often appear in clusters or drifts rather than as isolated individuals.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Blooms appear in loose clusters of 5-10 flowers per stem, with each flower having six pointed petals that spread flat and wide. The petals have a papery texture and often show delicate darker veining.

habitat: In New England, you'll find Boissier's Glory-of-the-snow naturalized in parks, old gardens, and around historic homes where it was originally planted and has spread. It thrives in well-drained soil under deciduous trees or in partially shaded areas that get good spring sunlight before the tree canopy fills in. Look for it in rich, loamy soil that doesn't stay waterlogged in winter.

seasonality.spring: Peak blooming time from March through early April, with flowers appearing before or just as leaves emerge. This is the only time of year you'll see this plant above ground, making spring identification crucial.
seasonality.summer: Completely dormant with no visible parts above ground. Leaves yellow and die back by late May, and the plant retreats to its underground bulb for the rest of the growing season.
seasonality.fall: Still dormant underground with no visible signs. The bulb is developing next year's flower buds during this period, but there's nothing to identify at the surface.
seasonality.winter: Remains completely dormant as a bulb below the frost line. No above-ground parts are visible, though very late in winter you might spot the first green shoots pushing through snow or leaf litter.

funFact: This little flower is such an early riser that it can actually generate its own heat to melt snow! Like other early spring bulbs, it can raise its internal temperature several degrees above the surrounding air, creating tiny warm microclimates that help it bloom even when frost threatens.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with Siberian squill, which has similar blue star-shaped flowers at the same time of year. The key difference is that Boissier's Glory-of-the-snow flowers face upward like they're looking at the sky, while Siberian squill flowers nod downward like little blue bells. Remember: "Glory looks up to the sky, squills look down and are shy."
contextualKnowledge: This species was originally classified in a separate genus called Chionodoxa (literally meaning "snow glory" in Greek), and you'll still see it sold under that name in garden centers. Botanists have recently moved it into the Scilla genus based on genetic research, but the name change is still working its way into popular use.
compareHints: Compared to its close relative Siberian squill, Boissier's Glory-of-the-snow has upward-facing flowers rather than nodding ones, and tends to have paler blue coloration with more prominent white centers. Forbes' Glory-of-the-snow is nearly identical but typically has larger flowers and may bloom slightly later. All the glory-of-the-snow species (former Chionodoxa) can be distinguished from true Scilla species by their upward-facing flowers and the way their petals are fused at the base rather than completely separate.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its squill relatives, Siberian squill is distinguished by its intense blue color and nodding flower habit.
Among the squills, Forbes' glory-of-the-snow stands out with its white-centered flowers and star shape, while Siberian squill has solid blue, more bell-shaped blooms.

Among the squills, Mishchenko squill stands out for its very pale blue flowers with dark veining, while Siberian squill has solid bright blue flowers and Alpine squill typically has just two leaves per bulb.
Alpine squill differs from its cousin Siberian squill by having exactly two leaves instead of three or four, and typically fewer flowers per stem.
